Today, the average rate on a 30Y mortgage surged by +17 basis points, to 7.45%.

This is the highest since November 2023.

Early-2023 came with 6%+ inflation, rate hikes, and an economy recovering from pandemic stimulus.

Mortgage rates are seemingly back in a similar position. https://t.co/fsGijXHxtJ

8 days ago, the Fed released their first unanimous decision since May 2025.

They hiked rates and were fully unified on it, even after months of dissents in favor of cuts.

"The Committee will deliver price stability," the Fed said.

This was a clear signal to the market. https://t.co/xhhf8lX1bq

This decision was more than a 25 basis point hike, it was a statement.

The Fed and Fed Chair Warsh made it clear that they are committed to their 2% inflation target and political pressure won't change that.

Now, markets are pricing in 100 basis points of hikes by next summer. https://t.co/o0d8Sqodgq

But, the question is, what changed over the last few days?

In our view, the market is now taking the Fed more seriously.

For months, markets were hesitant to price-in rate hikes because Fed Chair Warsh was appointed by Trump specifically to CUT rates.

That changed 8 days ago. https://t.co/kamLpDy4PI

So, what's happening?

At its core, inflation is the issue.

Brent crude oil prices are back above $105/barrel and diesel prices are at record highs.

US consumers expect inflation to rise to ~4.6% over the next year, the 3rd-highest reading in 12 months.

But, there's more. https://t.co/A35rt4VEGa

The surge in diesel prices comes in the midst of peak diesel demand season globally.

Global diesel consumption rises by 2 million barrels/day during this period.

Truckers are paying +100% more for fuel than they were 9 months ago.

4% inflation is low in this backdrop. https://t.co/BK5TWoKVJK

BREAKING: Institutional investors bought +$4.1 billion in US equities in the week ending September 18th.

This marks their 3rd weekly purchase over the last 4 weeks.

As a result, the 4-week average of institutional purchases rose to +$2.9 billion.

At the same time, hedge funds purchased +$1.2 billion, bringing their 4-week average of purchases up to +$1.6 billion.

Meanwhile, retail investors sold -$2.2 billion last week, posting their 8th consecutive weekly sale.

Retail investors have now sold an average of -$1.9 billion in US equities per week over the last 4 weeks.

Institutions are buying while retail is selling.

BREAKING: The S&P Global US Composite PMI index jumped +2.4 points in September, to 58.4, its highest reading since July 2021.

This also marks the 4th consecutive monthly improvement in growth.

This was driven by the services sector, with its index rising +2.2 points, to 58.7, its highest level since October 2021.

At the same time, Manufacturing PMI surged +3.1 points, to 57.0, its highest since May 2022.

Excluding the post-2020 pandemic reopening surge in demand, the latest improvement in business activity is the strongest since 2015.

However, this growth comes amid severe supply chain bottlenecks and labor shortages, pushing backlogs sharply higher and adding to inflationary pressures.

Inflationary pressures are mounting.

Below is a longer view of real yields vs real potential GDP growth and R-Star. For the ever-rising debt burden to remain sustainable, it’s essential that economic growth remains above the country’s funding rate. Based on the CBO’s real potential growth rate of 2.5% (and falling below 2% in the coming years), that is no longer the case. Hopefully, the CBO projections are too low given the AI boom that is currently underway. If not, we run the risk that the rising cost of capital will choke off the economy’s formidable growth. Note below that the last few times that the real yield spiked to or above the real potential growth rate were 2007, 2000, and 1994. Those were either rate shocks or growth shocks.
